name: Hot Take
description: A provocative, opinionated post that challenges conventional wisdom in the domain.
promptGuidance: Write this as a BOLD HOT TAKE — a provocative opinion that challenges conventional wisdom. The first line should be a strong claim that makes people stop scrolling. The second line should give one specific, concrete reason the claim is true. End with a short question or challenge. No hedging, no 'in my opinion', no 'some people say'.
example: Best practices are just survivor bias with better PR. The teams that win aren't following playbooks — they're running experiments the playbooks don't cover yet. What rule are you breaking this week?

name: Myth Buster
description: Correct a common misconception in the domain.
promptGuidance: Write this as a MYTH BUSTER — correct a common misconception. Start with the myth (state it as something people actually believe). Then immediately debunk it with a specific, verifiable fact or counter-example. End with a one-sentence takeaway that reframes the topic.
example: Myth: you need a big audience before you can monetize. Truth: a tiny, highly-trusted audience often outperforms a massive, low-trust one. Niche depth beats reach.

name: Specific Observation
description: A sharp, small observation that reveals a bigger pattern.
promptGuidance: Write this as a SPECIFIC OBSERVATION — one concrete, oddly specific detail from the topic that reveals a bigger pattern. The first line should name the specific thing. The next 1-2 lines should explain what it reveals. Avoid generalizations; the power is in the detail.
example: The best product teams don't ship features. They ship constraints. A new feature is a bet; a new constraint is a strategy.

name: Meme Energy
description: A post with meme-culture energy about the domain.
promptGuidance: Write this with MEME ENERGY — short, dry, internet-native. Use a relatable, low-stakes observation from the topic. Reference meme culture but keep it focused on the domain. The joke should land without explanation. No hashtags.
example: Me reading another '10x engineer' thread: 'tell me you never met a good manager without telling me you never met a good manager.'

name: Question Reveal
description: A rhetorical or direct question that reveals something about the topic.
promptGuidance: Write this as a QUESTION REVEAL — the first line is a question that sounds simple. The second line reveals why the answer is more interesting than it looks. The question should reveal something about the topic, not just ask for engagement.
example: Why do the fastest-growing tools always feel underwhelming at first? Because they're solving a problem the old guard doesn't think is a problem.

name: Story Bite
description: A personal or second-hand story that illustrates a point.
promptGuidance: Write this as a STORY BITE — a 2-3 sentence mini-story that makes a point. It can be personal, second-hand, or hypothetical, but it must feel specific and real. End with the insight, not the story summary.
example: A founder I know killed a feature users loved because the support cost was eating the whole team. The lesson: popularity is not profitability. Metrics without cost context are just vanity.

name: Tool Drop
description: A practical, useful mini-tip or resource.
promptGuidance: Write this as a TOOL DROP — a practical, useful mini-tip or resource. Lead with the concrete action or tool. One line on why it matters. No fluff, no CTA. The value should be obvious.
example: If your deployment pipeline takes more than 10 minutes, you're not shipping fast enough. Start by parallelizing tests before you buy more CI minutes.

name: Contrarian Kindness
description: A take that gently pushes back on a common belief while staying warm.
promptGuidance: Write this with CONTRARIAN KINDNESS — push back on a common belief, but stay warm and inviting. The disagreement should be about the idea, not the people who hold it. End with an inclusive thought or question.
example: Hustle culture isn't evil. It's just mispriced. Rest, reflection, and slow work are where most of the real gains hide.

name: One Weird Thing
description: A counter-intuitive pattern in the domain.
promptGuidance: Write this as ONE WEIRD THING — a counter-intuitive pattern in the domain. Lead with the surprising fact. Then one sentence explaining the mechanism. Then a short reflective question.
example: The best customer feedback rarely comes from power users. It comes from people who tried once, got confused, and quietly left. That's why churn surveys miss half the picture.

name: Curiosity Gap
description: A post that opens a gap and resolves it with a satisfying insight.
promptGuidance: Write this as a CURIOSITY GAP — first line opens a gap (something the reader wants to know). Second line gives a satisfying, specific answer. The resolution should feel worth the click, not anticlimactic.
example: Most teams overestimate how much their users notice new features. On average, 80% of users never discover a feature without in-app guidance. Build the guidance first.

name: Personal Win
description: A small, relatable win or realization.
promptGuidance: Write this as a PERSONAL WIN — a small, relatable win or realization. Keep it humble and specific. Avoid humble-bragging. The insight should be transferable to the reader.
example: I finally stopped optimizing for inbox zero and started optimizing for fewer decisions. Surprisingly, my output went up.

name: Mini Rant
description: A short, justified vent that the audience can relate to.
promptGuidance: Write this as a MINI RANT — a short, justified vent. The first line names the thing that annoys you. The next 1-2 lines explain why it's worse than people think. End with a sardonic one-liner or a call to do better.
example: Can we retire the phrase 'we're data-driven' when the data is just the last meeting's mood? If your chart has no confidence interval, it's a vibe check.
